strengths: Novel application of compressed sensing to attention head localization, achieving up to 50x fewer model evaluations than greedy baselines while maintaining comparable task-degradation efficacy (Table 4).

Broad empirical validation across 5 models spanning two model families (Llama, Qwen) and scales (1B-8B), and across 4 distinct capabilities (math, code, swearing, rhyming), lending some generality to the localization claims.

The generalization experiment (Table 3), showing heads identified on one dataset (e.g., GSM8K) transfer to degrade performance on a related dataset (Arithmetic), strengthens the claim that identified heads capture a genuine underlying capability rather than dataset-specific artifacts.
The discovery of 'universal heads' and scale-dependent localization (WMDP experiments) are interesting secondary findings that add nuance and open directions for future mechanistic work.
Clear problem formulation and algorithmic description (Section 3-4), with an ablation comparing Bernoulli vs. stratified sampling and different baselines, aiding reproducibility of the core method.
weaknesses: The additivity/linearity assumption underlying the compressed sensing formulation is only informally justified ('we assume...'); no direct empirical test comparing predicted additive effects vs. actual joint-ablation performance is presented to validate the core theoretical premise.

Head identification and hyperparameter selection (number of masks, sparsity) are both tuned per-task/per-model using the same 100-sample subset used to score candidate head sets, which risks overfitting the selection procedure to this exact subset; while final evaluation uses full datasets, the identification and hyperparameter tuning are not clearly separated from validation in a way that rules out subtle leakage or cherry-picking of hyperparameters per condition, which could bias comparisons against baselines that may not receive equivalent tuning effort.

Custom evaluation datasets for 'swearing' and 'rhyming' are minimally described (only 12 swearing prompts; rhyme dataset construction is vague and partly 'AI-assisted'), and profanity scoring via simple word-list matching is a coarse proxy for the intended capability, raising concerns about the reliability and reproducibility of two of the four core capability results.

No variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-run analysis is reported for any of the main results (Tables 2-5), making it difficult to assess whether reported degradations (e.g., -1.1 vs -2.3 in Gen columns) reflect real differences or noise, especially given small identification-time sample sizes.

The choice of exactly top-5 heads as the standard unit of analysis across all models/tasks is only loosely justified by a single plateau plot for math (Figure 2) on one model; it is unclear whether this fixed k is appropriate across the very different scales and head counts (512-1024) of the studied models.

The 'universal heads' phenomenon is reported only for Llama models and not observed in Qwen models, but this asymmetry is not explained or investigated, leaving an unresolved gap in the generality of this secondary claim.

Scale-dependence conclusions (Section 6.2) rest on only three models and a single benchmark family (WMDP/MMLU), which is a fairly thin evidentiary base for the strong claim that 'task-specific heads for specific knowledge may emerge only at larger scales.'

Minor but notable presentation issues suggest incomplete proofreading (e.g., Table 1 lists 'Qwen 2.5 3B and Qwen 2.5 3B' instead of 7B and 3B; the code repository link in the abstract is left blank), which slightly undermines confidence in reproducibility artifacts.

The paper does not compare against other established interpretability/localization baselines beyond internally-defined greedy search (e.g., gradient-based attribution, activation patching), limiting the ability to contextualize how much of the observed localization is a general property versus an artifact of the ablation-based measurement approach itself.

strengths: The core idea—framing attention-head importance recovery as a sparse linear inverse problem and applying compressed sensing machinery to cut the number of required model evaluations—is a sensible and reasonably novel application of an established tool to interpretability, distinct from prior work that requires finetuning (Chen et al., Panigrahi et al.) or exhaustive ablation.

The empirical sweep is reasonably broad: five models from two families (Llama, Qwen) spanning 1B-8B parameters, and four distinct capability types (math, code, swearing, rhyming), plus an additional WMDP knowledge-localization study.

The paper reports a useful practical finding (roughly consistent task-specific vs. general-task dissociation after ablating a handful of heads) and surfaces interesting secondary phenomena (universal heads, scale-dependent localization, GQA group clustering) that enrich the narrative beyond the main localization claim.

The writing and structure are clear, related work coverage is thorough and well organized along meaningful axes, and the method/algorithm description (Algorithm 1, matrix construction strategies) is reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: No uncertainty quantification anywhere: all tables report single point estimates (Δ Task, Δ Gen, accuracy) with no error bars, multiple random seeds for the compressed sensing measurement matrix, or significance testing, despite the method being explicitly randomized (Bernoulli/Stratified sampling) and evaluation using small subsets (100 samples) for head identification. Given the stochastic masking procedure, the stability of recovered head sets across seeds is never assessed.

The theoretical justification for applying compressed sensing is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be only 'informal': there is no verification of the restricted isometry/incoherence properties of Φ, no bound on the linearization error ϵ from the acknowledged highly nonlinear ablation interactions, and the diminishing-returns curve in Figure 2 (clear sub-additivity) arguably undercuts the paper's own additivity assumption rather than merely serving as motivation for choosing k=5.

Key supporting datasets (swearing, rhyming) are ad hoc, small (12 prompts for swearing), and evaluated with crude heuristics (profanity word-list matching, CMU rhyme dictionary), making the 'capability' claims for these tasks difficult to trust as evidence of a general phenomenon rather than artifacts of narrow prompt sets.

No random-ablation control baseline is reported (e.g., ablating random sets of 5 heads matched for location/count) to calibrate how surprising the task-specific degradation actually is relative to chance; the comparison is only against greedy/one-shot-greedy variants of the same general approach, not an independent null.

Hyperparameter selection for the compressed sensing method (number of masks, sparsity) is tuned by maximizing degradation on the same 100-sample subset later used (in aggregate full-dataset form) to report main results, risking subtle optimistic bias in the head-identification pipeline and method comparisons in Table 4.

The headline claims ('capability localization is a general organizational principle') are not well supported by the paper's own counter-evidence: WMDP shows only weak/absent localization in the 8B model, 'universal heads' and 'format-level' heads complicate the clean modularity story, and these secondary analyses (Section 6.1, 6.2) are based on only 1-4 models/heads with no systematic treatment, making the scale-dependence and universality claims largely anecdotal rather than rigorously established.

Generalization evidence (Table 3) is very thin—only two capability pairs (GSM8K/Arithmetic, MBPP/HumanEval) with no quantification of how much overlap in identified heads is expected by chance given N up to 1024 heads.

The paper offers no systematic ablation/robustness analysis of the Lasso regularization strength, no comparison of recovered head sets to a verified ground truth via exhaustive search for feasible (small) models to validate recovery fidelity, which would be the most convincing way to validate the central compressed-sensing claim.

strengths: The core idea of treating head importance as a sparse signal recoverable via compressed sensing is a novel and compute-efficient re-framing of causal head localization, with a well-motivated connection to known CS theory (sparsity + approximate additivity).

Reasonably broad empirical validation: 5 models spanning two families (Llama, Qwen) and sizes from 1B to 8B, and four distinct capability types (math, code, swearing, rhyming), with consistent qualitative findings across all of them.

Useful ablations: the paper directly compares the proposed stratified compressed-sensing method against greedy and one-shot-greedy baselines (Table 4), showing comparable task degradation with up to 50x fewer evaluations, which supports the central efficiency claim.

The paper goes beyond the main localization claim to report two additional, non-trivial phenomena (universal heads and scale-dependent localization on WMDP/MMLU), which enrich the contribution and open interesting follow-up questions.

Generalization checks across datasets measuring the same capability (GSM8K vs Arithmetic, MBPP vs HumanEval) and a specificity check against general benchmarks (HellaSwag, BoolQ, ARC-C, MMLU) help rule out trivial explanations like general model damage.

Reasonably detailed implementation/appendix information (hyperparameter search procedure, dataset subset sizes, custom task construction) supports partial reproducibility, and code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: The linear/additive approximation underlying the Lasso recovery (treating multi-head ablation effects as a sum of independent marginal effects) is asserted but never directly validated (e.g., no residual analysis, no comparison of predicted vs. actual multi-head ablation performance, no sensitivity analysis of how badly non-linearity corrupts recovery as more heads are jointly ablated).

Head identification relies on only 100-sample subsets and a single run per setting; no variance/confidence intervals are reported across random seeds or alternate subsamples for either the measurement matrix sampling or the resulting head sets, making it hard to assess the stability/reliability of the recovered heads.

The 'swearing' and 'rhyming' tasks rely on small, custom, seemingly ad hoc datasets with simplistic evaluation metrics (raw profanity word counts, rhyme pair lists built with 'manual and AI-assisted curation'); these are not validated against existing benchmarks or human judgments, weakening confidence in the generalizability of findings tied to these tasks.

The choice of k=5 heads is justified mainly by a qualitative 'plateauing' argument (Figure 2) rather than a principled stopping criterion, and the degree of localization reported (e.g., -16 to -65% depending on model/task) varies widely, undercutting the strength of claims about 'extreme' localization as a general principle.

Broad claims in the abstract/conclusion that 'capability localization is a general organizational principle of Transformer language models' are not fully supported by evidence restricted to two closely related model families (Llama, Qwen) and a narrow set of capabilities; no negative controls or capabilities for which localization fails are discussed (except briefly for WMDP in the largest model).

The WMDP (hazardous knowledge) results and the general framing of the method for 'targeted model editing' and 'AI safety' raise a dual-use concern (identifying and potentially removing/retaining specific hazardous-knowledge circuits) that is not addressed in any ethics or broader impact discussion.

No comparison against alternative existing localization/attribution baselines beyond simple greedy ablation (e.g., gradient-based attribution, activation patching, or path patching methods commonly used in the interpretability literature), limiting the ability to judge the comparative advantage of the proposed approach beyond compute efficiency.

Minor inconsistencies in presentation, e.g., the model list states 'Qwen 2.5 3B and Qwen 2.5 3B' in the main text (likely a typo for 7B), which slightly undermines confidence in the care taken in reporting experimental details.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, well-motivated method for localizing task-specific attention heads using compressed sensing, grounded in a plausible sparsity + approximate linearity assumption, and connects nicely to compressed sensing theory (O(k log(N/k)) measurements).

Extensive empirical validation across 6 models (Llama and Qwen, 1B-14B) and 4 diverse capabilities (math, code, swearing, rhyming), with consistent findings that ablating ~5 heads produces large task-specific degradation while sparing general capabilities (Table 2).

Good ablation/ generalization checks: cross-dataset validation (GSM8K heads affect Arithmetic and vice versa; MBPP heads affect HumanEval), comparison against greedy/one-shot-greedy baselines and ProxySPEX showing large efficiency gains (up to 50x fewer evaluations) with comparable accuracy, random-head and mean-vs-zero ablation controls.

Interesting secondary findings (universal heads, scale-dependent localization, GQA head clustering, WMDP/MMLU shared format heads) that enrich the paper's contribution and open directions for future mechanistic study.

Reasonably strong connection to prior mechanistic interpretability findings (e.g., independently recovering L16H21/L15H13 identified by Nikankin et al. for arithmetic), lending some external validity to the method.
Detailed appendix with hyperparameter search procedures, full head lists, and additional ablations, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The additivity/first-order linearity assumption underlying the Lasso-based recovery is asserted rather than rigorously validated; the paper acknowledges nonlinearity but provides only indirect empirical support (i.e., that recovery works) rather than a direct test of how well the linear model fits actual joint-ablation effects.

The claimed formal compressed-sensing guarantees (M ≈ O(k log(N/k))) are invoked loosely ("informally motivates") without an accompanying restricted isometry property (RIP)-style justification for the specific binary/stratified measurement matrices used, weakening the theoretical rigor implied by the title/framing.

Recall@k results (Table 7) are quite low (0.2-0.53) even at 300 evaluations, indicating the method's agreement with greedy "ground truth" is modest; the paper's explanation (noise, near-equal importance of extra heads) is plausible but not independently verified, leaving open how faithful the identified head sets truly are beyond the top 1-2 heads.

Task diversity is somewhat narrow and includes two custom, small, and seemingly ad hoc datasets (12 swearing prompts, ~113 rhyming pairs) without inter-rater/robustness analysis of the automatic scoring (e.g., profanity-word matching, CMU-dict rhyme checking), raising concerns about noise/label quality reflected in the very large error bars for SWEAR (e.g., ±30.2 for Qwen-14B) and RHYME.

The necessity-but-not-sufficiency finding (retaining only task heads yields poor performance) is only briefly mentioned in the intro as a 'preliminary experiment' without quantitative results, circuit analysis, or discussion of what this implies for the causal interpretation of 'task-specific' heads.

Hyperparameters (number of masks, sparsity level) are tuned per model/dataset via a small grid search using the actual evaluation task performance as the selection criterion (Appendix A.2), which could inflate reported efficiency numbers and reduces the method's plug-and-play practicality; the sensitivity of results to this tuning is not clearly quantified.

The scale-dependence and WMDP findings (Section 6.2) are based on a single model pair comparison (Llama 3.1 8B vs. 3.2 3B/1B) and speculative interpretation ("format-specific vs task-specific"), which is an interesting but underpowered claim given only 2-3 data points across scale.

The Impact Statement is minimal/boilerplate given that the paper explicitly discusses AI safety and model editing implications (including techniques that could disable/degrade specific capabilities), which merits more substantive discussion of dual-use risks (e.g., using localized heads to degrade safety-relevant behaviors).

strengths: The empirical phenomenon demonstrated—that ablating a handful (as few as 2-5) of attention heads can severely degrade performance on a specific capability while leaving unrelated tasks largely intact—is interesting and is shown with reasonable breadth: 6 models from two families (Llama, Qwen) spanning 1B-14B parameters, and 4 distinct capabilities.

The compressed sensing approach offers a genuine and demonstrated efficiency gain over naive greedy search (e.g., 100-300 evaluations vs. 1024-5120 for Llama-3.1-8B), which is practically useful for interpretability workflows with large models.

Several sanity checks strengthen credibility of the core finding: random head ablation produces minimal degradation (Appendix B.2), zero- vs mean-ablation give similar results, and independently-discovered heads (L16H21, L15H13) match heads previously identified via careful manual mechanistic analysis in Nikankin et al. (2024) for arithmetic.

The paper reports several additional, intellectually interesting phenomena (universal heads, scale-dependent localization, GQA head clustering) that, while exploratory, add texture to the main contribution and suggest directions for future mechanistic work.

The related work section is thorough and appropriately positions the contribution relative to SPEX/ProxySPEX, ALPS, HeadMap, and classical attention-head interpretability literature, including an honest discussion of what is and isn't novel relative to ProxySPEX.
weaknesses: The method's reliability is self-undermined by the paper's own recall analysis (Table 7): Recall@5 against the greedy 'ground truth' is only 0.333-0.533 even at the largest evaluation budget tested, meaning the compressed-sensing method often returns a different head set than greedy search. The paper explains this away post-hoc (claiming only 2 heads really matter) rather than treating it as a validity concern for the core identification claim.

The additivity/linearity assumption underlying the compressed-sensing formulation is asserted only informally ('informally motivates') and is in tension with the paper's own observation that ablating all task-specific heads together ('retaining only the task-specific heads') yields much worse performance than expected under a simple additive model—this nonlinearity is acknowledged but never quantified or reconciled with the Lasso-based recovery guarantees invoked.

The 'necessary but not sufficient' framing and the finding that task heads 'do not make up a self-contained circuit' is a significant qualification to the central localization claim, yet it is relegated to a brief paragraph with no quantitative characterization (e.g., how much of the task is explained by the top-k heads vs. residual computation), weakening the significance of the 'modular organization' narrative promoted in the abstract/conclusion.

Several key evaluation tasks are custom, small, and loosely validated (12 hand-written swearing prompts, ~113 rhyme pairs), used both for head discovery and (partially) for reporting final results; these are not standard benchmarks and the paper gives minimal detail on how robust/validated these custom metrics are, raising concerns about the generality of 'rhyming' and 'swearing' as representative 'capabilities.'

Variance across seeds is very large for several results (e.g., SWEAR ∆ for Qwen-2.5-14B: −32.6 ± 30.2; Llama-3.2-3B: −36.0 ± 16.0), to the point where confidence intervals span most of the effect size, yet these noisy results are still used to support claims of consistent, strong localization.

The comparison to ProxySPEX (Section 6.4) is not a fair or complete comparison: ProxySPEX is run at reduced budget (500 vs. the original paper's 5000) and restricted to a 96-head, 3-layer subset chosen in the original paper, while the proposed method searches the full 1024-head space—the claimed parity is drawn from a single task/model pair with mismatched search spaces.

The hyperparameter tuning procedure (Appendix A.1-A.2) requires per-model, per-task search over mask count and sparsity using validation evaluations on 100-sample subsets, which is not accounted for in the headline '50x fewer evaluations' efficiency claims; the true end-to-end cost of applying this method to a new task/model is understated.

The WMDP/scale-dependence analysis (Section 6.2) draws fairly strong conclusions ('task-specific heads may emerge only at larger scales') from a single model per scale bucket and single/double heads identified post-hoc, which is a thin evidentiary basis for a claimed general scale-dependence phenomenon.

The paper lacks comparison against simpler, well-established attribution baselines (e.g., gradient-based attribution, attention-weight analysis) beyond the greedy ablation baselines it introduces itself, making it harder to assess whether compressed sensing's efficiency gains come at a meaningful accuracy cost relative to other feasible alternatives.

strengths: Broad and systematic empirical validation across six models spanning two families (Llama, Qwen) and a wide parameter range (1B–14B), and across four distinct capabilities (math, code, profanity, rhyming) plus an additional WMDP knowledge benchmark, lending credibility to the general claim of capability localization.

The compressed-sensing approach is a genuinely useful methodological contribution: it reduces the number of required model evaluations by up to 50x relative to greedy search while achieving comparable task-specific degradation, which has practical value for interpretability research at scale.

Thorough set of control experiments: comparison of zero vs. mean ablation, a random-head-ablation baseline showing minimal effect, hyperparameter search documentation (masks/sparsity) in the appendix, and a direct comparison against a recent related method (ProxySPEX).

Cross-dataset generalization checks (e.g., GSM8K-identified heads also degrade Arithmetic, MBPP-identified heads degrade HumanEval) strengthen the claim that identified heads correspond to genuine capability-level mechanisms rather than dataset-specific artifacts.

Interesting auxiliary findings (universal heads, scale-dependent localization, format-based 'knowledge MC' heads in smaller models) that are independently interesting and connect to existing mechanistic interpretability literature (e.g., independently recovering heads identified by Nikankin et al. for arithmetic), adding external validity.

The paper is honest about limitations of the approach, e.g., explicitly noting identified heads are necessary but not sufficient, that recall relative to greedy search is imperfect, and that the top-5 selection is a conservative overestimate due to noise.
weaknesses: The core sparsity/additivity assumption underlying the compressed sensing formulation is justified only informally and via overall empirical success; there is no direct measurement of how well first-order linear effects actually approximate multi-head ablation outcomes (e.g., comparing predicted vs. actual joint-ablation performance), leaving the theoretical grounding somewhat thin relative to the strength of the claims made.

Recall@k results against the greedy 'ground truth' are quite low (0.2–0.667 across budgets), which raises concerns about the reliability/stability of the specific heads recovered, even though the paper offers a plausible explanation (only 1-2 heads truly matter, rest is noise); this explanation is not independently verified.

The custom swearing (12 prompts) and rhyming datasets are very small, making the corresponding quantitative results (especially the noisy, high-variance swearing numbers in Table 2) less statistically convincing than the standard benchmark results.

The WMDP localization results for the largest model (Llama 3.1 8B) are weak/inconsistent with the paper's central claim of strong localization, and the explanation for scale-dependence (format-specific heads at smaller scale) is based on very few models/heads and largely qualitative analysis.

The ProxySPEX comparison is limited to a single task/model pair and run at a reduced budget relative to the original paper due to compute constraints, which weakens the strength of the efficiency comparison conclusion.
The choice of ablating exactly five heads is somewhat arbitrary and acknowledged to overestimate the true sparse set in many cases, complicating precise interpretation of the main results table.

The Impact Statement is minimal and does not meaningfully engage with dual-use or safety risks despite the paper explicitly motivating applications to 'AI safety' and the ease with which the method could be used to surgically disable model capabilities (or potentially safety-relevant behaviors).

All experiments use instruction-tuned models only; no analysis of whether localization patterns hold similarly for base (non-instruct) models, which limits the generality of the scale-dependence and universal-head claims.
